meta.title: Same Notes, Different Home
meta.summary: A note set has no key of its own — the bass, the chords, and where a phrase lands and stops are what make seven shared notes sound like C major or like A minor.

spans.text: "A minor is just C major starting on A" gets half of this right and stops there. Right: the notes really are the same seven. Wrong: starting the same scale from a different note does not, by itself, make anything sound minor. A set of notes has no key of its own — it's just seven pitches sitting there, waiting to be pointed somewhere, and pointing them takes more than picking a different starting letter.

What decides whether seven notes sound like C major or like A minor is not the note list — it's what the music leans on. This is well established: a listener's sense of home comes from duration and repetition, from what the harmony and the bass carry, not from which pitches are technically available. Four things, in practice, do the deciding:

items.text: What the chords underneath are built from
Which note a phrase keeps landing on
Which note the music stops on

spans.text: None of that is guesswork, and it is close to how this app's own key detector scores a progression: the chords themselves count for more than the bare list of pitches, and where a chord sits in the loop — first, last — counts on top of that. Which is why the same seven notes can come out as two different keys.

Here's the demonstration, and it's the centre of this lesson. Two four-chord loops, built from nothing but the seven notes C major and A minor share, differing only in which chord opens and closes the loop:

props.caption: The major loop — opens and closes on C
The minor loop — same middle two chords, opens and closes on Am

One honest limit, because none of this should be oversold: a bare scale run or a two-chord loop can be genuinely ambiguous, and the loops above were picked precisely because they aren't. Real music settles the question with time, repetition, and where the phrase actually stops — the same four things named above, just at the scale of a whole song instead of a four-bar loop.
